accused_occupation: Film distributor (business run in the name of a films distribution firm)
statutory_provisions: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 s.138 (read with s.139 presumption)
evidence_type: Documentary (cheque and signature, bank return memo) with statutory presumption under s.139; complainant's testimony on loan
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.138 NI Act; fine Rs.5,55,000, in default five months simple imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Criminal revision allowed; judgments of both lower courts set aside and accused acquitted
offence_finally_established: Dishonour of cheque under Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
neutral_facts: The complainant, who owned a cinema theatre, and the accused, who distributed films, had a business relationship in which the accused supplied films to the theatre for screening. In May 2006 the accused asked the complainant for a loan of five lakh rupees to support the making of a Tamil film, and the complainant advanced the money on 20 May 2006. The accused promised to repay the loan on the film's release but did not repay it. After repeated requests, the accused issued a cheque for five lakh rupees dated 16 January 2007, drawn on a bank in Bangalore. The complainant presented the cheque through his bank the same day, and it was returned on 18 January 2007 with the remark 'Stop Payment'. The complainant then sent a legal notice on 27 January 2007 to the accused's office and residential addresses. The residential notice was received under RPAD, while the office notice was returned marked 'Absent-Information delivered'. The accused did not pay or respond. The accused's account was that the business was run by the accused's husband, that the accused denied taking any loan, and that the cheque had been given in 1999 as security for an earlier loan, which was repaid. According to the accused, the complainant had not returned that cheque, claiming it was misplaced, and later used it out of ill will arising from a dispute over the release of a film in the complainant's theatre. The cheque leaf bore a printed date reading '199_'. The signature and the cheque itself were not disputed.
financial_property_loss: Rs 5,00,000 loan amount and cheque amount claimed as unpaid
motive: alleged: complainant's ill will over release of film 'Pokari' led him to use an old cheque for revenge
key_evidence_accepted: Cheque and accused's signature (not disputed); dishonour by 'Stop Payment' implying the accused knew of presentation; s.139 presumption
witness_credibility: Accused's 1999 security-cheque story rejected as unworthy of credit and unsupported by evidence; printed date on cheque not conclusive
trial_duration: offence: 16-01-2007 (cheque issued), 18-01-2007 (cheque dishonoured); trial judgment: not given; High Court: 22-07-2011; Supreme Court: April 28, 2015
legal_representation: Appellant (complainant): Rajesh Mahale, Krutin R. Joshi. Respondent (accused): Kiran Suri, Apurva Upamanyu, Dr. Vipin Gupta. No State counsel noted.
investigation_status: Complaint filed; legal notice served; trial completed before Magistrate
procedural_irregularity: High Court wrongly placed the burden of proof on the complainant instead of the accused under s.139
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted; Fast Track Court (appeal): conviction upheld; High Court (revision): acquitted; Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction restored
prosecution_argument: Not stated (judgment does not separately record the complainant's submissions; it notes the controversy on whether the complainant must first prove a legally enforceable debt)
defence_argument: Not separately recorded in SC judgment; accused's position was that the cheque was a 1999 security cheque, the loan was repaid, and the cheque was misused out of ill will
legal_principle_applied: Section 139 presumption is rebuttable; once cheque and signature are admitted, the burden shifts to accused to disprove the cheque or any legally recoverable debt
